name: The Waldhaustanne (Zwieslerwaldhaus Silver Fir)

location.address: Bayerischer Wald National Park, near Zwieslerwaldhaus, on the forest path from the Brechhaeuslau car park towards Schwellhaeusl, about 1,360m elevation below the Grosser Rachel summit

access: Free. Inside Bayerischer Wald National Park (Germany's oldest national park), on a forest path roughly 500m from the Brechhaeuslau car park; a wooden boardwalk protects the root zone, so visitors stay on the walkway rather than approaching the trunk directly.
transport: No train/bus station nearby; reached via the Brechhaeuslau car park near Zwieslerwaldhaus, then a c. 500m walk on a marked forest path.
verify_notes: IDENTIFICATION NOTE: the source lead's name was 'Nationalerbe-Baum' (49.099083, 13.23), which is the name of a nationwide designation programme (Germany's National Heritage Trees, run by the Deutsche Dendrologische Gesellschaft / DDG), not a specific tree's given name; the Commons category behind the lead had mixed in photos of at least two unrelated Nationalerbe-Baeume (a Bremen cemetery mammoth tree and a Homberg/Ohm lime, both far from these coordinates). The coordinate itself pins exactly to this silver fir: nationalerbe-baeume.de's own project page gives GPS 49.098683/13.230611, matching to within about 50m. SINGLE-TREE-DESTINATION CASE: this is Germany's tallest, thickest and oldest documented silver fir (Abies alba), roughly 605 years old, girth 6.93m (measured Jan 2023), height about 53m, discovered for the register in 2020 by a visiting family and verified by Prof. Dr. Andreas Roloff (TU Dresden) for the DDG; named National Heritage Tree No. 26 on 23 June 2023. A 2023 survey found 274 species living in and on the tree. It stands in an old-growth fir stand about 1.5km from the Czech border inside the Bayerischer Wald National Park, Germany's oldest and one of its largest protected forests (contiguous with the Czech Sumava). Two independent official sources agree closely on all figures: the DDG's own nationalerbe-baeume.de project page and the national park administration's press release. This clears the 2026-08-31 single-tree exception easily: a documented national and dendrological record-holder inside a named national park is exactly the kind of destination someone would travel specifically to see.

name: The Volkenrodaer Koenigseiche
age_estimate: roughly 600 years (locally called the "1000-year oak", which the tree register itself calls popular exaggeration)

location.address: Am Pfingstrasen, edge of Volkenroda, a district of Koerner, Unstrut-Hainich district, Thuringia

access: Free, on public/open ground at the edge of the village.
transport: No station nearby; Volkenroda is a small village reached by road, walkable from the village centre and the former Kloster Volkenroda monastery grounds.
verify_notes: SINGLE-TREE-DESTINATION CASE, small village with nothing else nearby. Also called the Koenigseiche or Dicke Eiche. One of the thickest oaks in Germany: girth 9.8m measured 30 June 2019 (baumkunde.de), height 23m, vital as of a September 2022 check. Popularly called the 'Tausendjaehrige Eiche' (1000-year oak) but the register itself calls that an exaggeration; scientific dating (a 1992 core sample combined with 19th-century circumference records, per an older account) puts the age at roughly 500-600 years, baumkunde.de's own register text saying about 600. Believed to be a relic wood-pasture oak from the heyday of the nearby Cistercian Kloster Volkenroda; one source (search summary, not independently re-verified on this pass) says the site is referenced in monastery documents from the 12th century, while baumkunde.de's own text says 10th century -- SOURCES CONFLICT on this specific century and neither figure was verified against the primary document, so treat the monastery-era connection as attested but the exact century as unresolved. A lightning strike in 1989 broke a main branch, which is what allowed scientific age determination. Repairs/conservation work happened in 1955 and 1991, each time with a note in a bottle left inside the tree. Naturdenkmal and Baumveteran designated tree. Two independent sources agree on name, species, coordinates and the headline girth/height figures: baumkunde.de's tree register and monumentale-eichen.de (Rainer Lippert's monumental oaks site).

name: The Tausendjaehrige Eiche of Boetersheim
age_estimate: roughly 600-800 years (the "1000-year" name is a local nickname, not a documented age)

location.address: Beside Esteweg 1, next to the war memorial (Kriegerdenkmal), Boetersheim, a hamlet of Kakenstorf, Landkreis Harburg, Lower Saxony

access: Free, publicly accessible next to the village war memorial.
transport: No station nearby; Boetersheim is a small hamlet (roughly 150 residents) reached by road, on the Bahndamm-route cycling/walking trail from the Landkreis Harburg.
verify_notes: SINGLE-TREE-DESTINATION CASE: a genuinely dramatic veteran oak, one of the largest in Lower Saxony, standing beside a war memorial in a tiny, picturesque hamlet that also has an old watermill and smithy. Girth recorded as 7.10m (alte-baeume-der-heide.de, undated recent survey) and 7.3m (baumkunde.de, measured 10 Aug 2016); this record uses 710cm as the more recent figure but both are consistent with a genuinely huge trunk. Height 21m (2023 measurement per a search summary of a since-unreachable page) to 23m (baumkunde.de, 2016); crown diameter about 14m. AGE CONFLICT, flagged rather than silently resolved: baumkunde.de and alte-baeume-der-heide.de both give 600-800 years; one early web-search AI summary on this pass separately surfaced a '350 years' figure that could not be traced to a specific fetched page and does not match either primary register consulted directly, so it is recorded here as discarded per the search-summary caution rule rather than used. Popularly called the 'Tausendjaehrige Eiche' but both registers call that a nickname rather than a documented age. History: struck by lightning and smouldered for weeks in the early 20th century, an old local account timing a bark-burning incident to around 1904; the trunk burst in 1959 and a large branch broke off. Today the trunk is completely hollow, heavily fissured and full of decayed wood (Mulm); it is stabilised with steel cables/props at the top. Both consulted sources agree it is currently ALIVE and vital-though-declining as of their most recent surveys (baumkunde.de's underlying data reflects a 2023 revisit per a search summary; alte-baeume-der-heide.de is undated but recent). Two independent sources: baumkunde.de's tree register and alte-baeume-der-heide.de (a dedicated local old-trees-of-the-Heide site).
